info.name: POCOR-9697 — super_admin escalation tests
info.description:
Side-by-side regression suite for the super_admin privilege-escalation vulnerability.

**How to use this collection for the video:**
1. Record once on the *master* branch — tests will FAIL (red), proving the exploit works.
2. Deploy POCOR-9697, then record again — same tests now PASS (green).

Each request:
  - performs the attack (or checks the leaky surface)
  - asserts the SAFE (post-fix) behavior

So "red on master, green on branch" is the whole story.

**Setup before recording:**
  - In Postman → File → Settings → uncheck "SSL certificate verification" (local cert is self-signed).
  - Edit collection variables `base_url`, `username`, `password`, `api_key` for your environment.
  - Run the requests in order — later requests depend on tokens/IDs set by earlier ones.

**POCOR-9697 — Read-side _conditions allowlist (items 09a–09d):**
Even with `$hidden` stripping the value from response bodies, an attacker could enumerate super_admins via membership inference on `_conditions`. POCOR-9697 closes this with a per-model `$fillable - $hidden` column allowlist in `CrudApiController` that silently drops unknown / hidden fields (no 422, no field-name leak, structured server-side log only). Items 09a–09d codify the threat model: 09a fires the attack, 09b proves the clause was dropped (totals match), 09c does the same for the password oracle, 09d proves we did not over-restrict legitimate clients.

item.name: 00 — Setup: Login as admin

request.description: Acquires the JWT used by every subsequent request. Also seeds a unique username (`exploit_<ms>`) so the test can be re-run without DB collisions.

item.name: 01 — v4 ATTACK: mass-assign super_admin (silent strip, 200 + DB super_admin=0)

request.description:
The exploit. Sends super_admin:1 to POST /api/v4/users.

**On master (BEFORE fix):** returns 200, row created with super_admin=1 — the attacker wins.
**On POCOR-9697 (AFTER fix):** also returns 200 — but the field was silently stripped by prepareForValidation(). The attempt is logged server-side to storage/logs/laravel.log. The response body MUST NOT contain the string 'super_admin' (would fingerprint the field for attackers).

exec: pm.test('Request looks like normal success (200)', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));
pm.test('FIX: response body does NOT name super_admin (no fingerprint)', () => {
// Capture the created user id so the next test can verify DB state without naming the field.
else { console.log('v4 create did not return id — DB verification will be skipped'); }

item.name: 02 — v4 ATTACK: elevate existing admin via id (silent strip, no fingerprint)

request.description: Variant of the exploit that targets an existing user (here id=2). Same silent-strip applies on the update path. Response must NOT mention super_admin. Admin row's super_admin stays at 1 (it was already 1 before the request and the update path drops the field, so the column is untouched).

exec: pm.test('Request looks like normal success (200)', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));
pm.test('FIX: response body does NOT name super_admin', () => {

item.name: 03 — v5 ATTACK: mass-assign super_admin (must succeed but DB super_admin=0)

request.description:
v5 CRUD: the request itself succeeds (201) because we hold add permission. The interesting question is whether super_admin:1 from the body was persisted.

**On master:** super_admin=1 is persisted (model has it in $fillable).
**On POCOR-9697:** super_admin is no longer fillable — the field is silently dropped, row created with super_admin=0. Verified by the next request, which logs in as the new user and checks /permissions.

item.name: 04 — Login as the new v5 user (proves password was hashed)

request.description:
Logs in as the user we just created. Login only works if the password column contains a valid bcrypt hash of the plaintext we sent — which proves the model's setPasswordAttribute mutator (or the repository's helper, for v4) hashed it on write.

**On master:** depends — model's $fillable also has password, so the value goes in raw — login FAILS. On POCOR-9697 the mutator hashes it and login SUCCEEDS.

exec: pm.test('FIX: new user can log in (password was hashed on write)', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));

item.name: 05 — /permissions for new user (must show super_admin = 0)

request.description:
GET /api/v4/permissions returns the CALLER's own super_admin flag (this endpoint is intentionally allowed to do so — the frontend reads it for UI gating).

**On master:** super_admin is 1 — the v5 mass-assignment succeeded.
**On POCOR-9697:** super_admin is 0 — model dropped the field on write.

exec: console.log('super_admin flag for new user =', sa);
pm.test('FIX: new user is NOT super_admin', () => pm.expect(Number(sa)).to.equal(0));

item.name: 06 — INFO LEAK: GET /api/v4/users/{id} must not contain super_admin or password

request.description: Visit the user-detail endpoint as admin. Before the fix this response leaked both `super_admin` and the bcrypt `password` hash in the response body (UserService::getUsersData built the response array manually, bypassing the model's $hidden).

exec: pm.test('FIX: response has no super_admin key', () => pm.expect(userData).to.not.have.property('super_admin'));
pm.test('FIX: response has no password key',    () => pm.expect(userData).to.not.have.property('password'));

item.name: 07 — INFO LEAK: POST /api/v4/users/basic-information must not contain super_admin or password

request.description: Directory search endpoint. Before the fix, DirectoryRepository::getUserByBasicInfo manually copied super_admin into every result row. The query already filtered super_admin != 1, so the leaked value was always 0 — but exposing the field at all is needless information disclosure and would surprise a security review.

exec: if (rows.length === 0) pm.test('no rows returned — still asserts shape on next non-empty run', () => pm.expect(true).to.equal(true));

item.name: 08 — SWAGGER LEAK: /api-docs-v4.json must have ≤1 super_admin hits

request.description:
The public swagger JSON. Before the fix and pre-regeneration, this file contained 6 super_admin entries — including the worst-case `"example": 1` that effectively documented the exploit for any reader.

**On master (or any deploy that skipped the swagger-regen post-deploy step):** ≥ 6 hits.
**On POCOR-9697 with proper deploy:** exactly 1 hit (the legitimate /api/v4/permissions self-introspection response).

exec: pm.test('FIX: at most 1 super_admin hit (the /permissions self-introspection)', () => pm.expect(hits).to.be.at.most(1));

item.name: 09 — SWAGGER LEAK: /api-docs-v5.json must have 0 super_admin hits

request.description: v5 has no legitimate super_admin response anywhere, so the count must be zero after the fix.

item.name: 09a — READ-SIDE ATTACK: enumerate super_admin via _conditions (must be silently dropped)

request.description: Even with `$hidden` stripping `super_admin` from response bodies, an attacker could enumerate super_admins via membership inference on `_conditions`: the WHERE clause runs server-side and the returned row IDs leak who is in the set. POCOR-9697 closes this with a per-model column allowlist (`getFillable()` minus `getHidden()`) in CrudApiController. The clause is silently dropped — no 422, no field-name leak — and the response total matches the unfiltered baseline.

exec: pm.test('Request returns 200 (no fingerprint via error)', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));
pm.test('FIX: response body does not name the dropped field (no fingerprint)', () => {

item.name: 09b — READ-SIDE BASELINE: unfiltered total (proves the clause was dropped, not applied)

request.description: Baseline unfiltered total. The previous request's total must match this one — if it does, the `_conditions=super_admin:1` clause was dropped (the whole table came back). If it is smaller, the clause leaked through and we have not closed the hole.

exec: console.log('baseline total =', baseline, '| blocked clause total =', blocked);
pm.test('FIX: dropped-clause total equals unfiltered baseline (no membership inference)', () => {

item.name: 09c — READ-SIDE ATTACK: password binary-search oracle via _conditions (must be silently dropped)

request.description: On master, `_conditions=password:>$2y$` runs as a real SQL WHERE clause, letting an attacker binary-search the bcrypt hash one byte at a time (the 'live PoC returned 113 confirmed real-hashed users' in the audit). POCOR-9697 drops the clause silently — total matches baseline, and the response body must not name the dropped field.

exec: pm.test('Request returns 200 (no DB error fingerprint)', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));
pm.test('FIX: total matches the unfiltered baseline (oracle neutralised)', () => {
pm.test('FIX: response does not contain a "password" key (no oracle leak)', () => {

item.name: 09d — READ-SIDE SANITY: legitimate $fillable column still filters

request.description: The fix must not regress legitimate clients. `username` is in `$fillable` and not in `$hidden`, so `_conditions=username:admin` must still filter as before — proving we did not over-restrict the read surface.

exec: pm.test('Legitimate filter still narrows the result set', () => {

item.name: AUDIT-1 — Audit-trail forgery: v5 create with forged created_user_id (must be overwritten with JWT user)

request.description: POCOR-9697 Wave-2: v5 create path must derive created_user_id / modified_user_id from the authenticated JWT user, never from the request body. Sending 99999 must be silently overwritten (server log + persisted JWT user id). The response must not echo the field names in any error/diagnostic context (anti-fingerprinting).

exec: pm.test('FIX: persisted created_user_id is NOT 99999 (forgery neutralised)', () => {
pm.test('FIX: response body does not name the forgery (no fingerprint)', () => {

item.name: AUDIT-2 — Audit-trail forgery: v5 update with forged modified_user_id (must be overwritten)

request.description: POCOR-9697 Wave-2: v5 update path must always overwrite modified_user_id with the JWT user. The follow-up GET (AUDIT-3) re-fetches the row to confirm it landed as the caller, not 99999.

item.name: AUDIT-3 — Audit-trail forgery: re-read user and assert modified_user_id is JWT user, created_user_id unchanged

request.description: Confirms AUDIT-2: re-fetch the user and verify modified_user_id is NOT 99999. Also re-confirms created_user_id is immutable — a follow-up PUT below tries to change it and we re-read again.

exec: pm.test('FIX: modified_user_id is NOT 99999 (overwritten from JWT)', () => {

item.name: AUDIT-4 — Audit-trail forgery: v5 update with forged created_user_id (must be silently stripped, original preserved)

request.description: POCOR-9697 Wave-2: created_user_id is immutable. Sending it on update must be silently stripped + logged; the row's original creator must remain unchanged.

item.name: AUDIT-5 — Audit-trail forgery: re-read user and assert created_user_id unchanged from original

request.description: Final confirmation that created_user_id is immutable. Compared against the value captured in AUDIT-3.

exec: pm.test('FIX: created_user_id is unchanged (immutable, forgery dropped)', () => {

item.name: WAVE3-1 — Audit log: create a fresh v5 user and capture id

request.description: Wave 3 (POCOR-9697): create a user via v5 and capture its id for the subsequent audit-log assertions. The trait UserActivityLog must drop a row into user_activities for this create.

item.name: WAVE3-2 — Audit log: GET /api/v5/user-activities for the new user (create row must exist)

request.description: Wave 3 (POCOR-9697): the trait must have produced a 'create' row in user_activities for the user just created. The response must NEVER contain a literal password or bcrypt hash.

exec: pm.test('FIX: at least one create-row exists for the new user', () => {
pm.test('FIX: no audit row leaks a bcrypt hash or plaintext password', () => {

item.name: WAVE3-3 — Audit log: PUT to change first_name + email then re-GET activities

request.description: Wave 3 (POCOR-9697): updating two ordinary fields must produce one user_activities row per dirty field. Verified in the next request.

item.name: WAVE3-4 — Audit log: confirm per-dirty-field update rows are present

request.description: Wave 3 (POCOR-9697): the trait must have emitted one update row for first_name and one for email.

exec: pm.test('FIX: update rows include first_name + email', () => {
pm.test('FIX: password/super_admin never appear as field names here', () => {

item.name: 10 — Cleanup: delete the demo v5 user (best-effort)

request.description: Best-effort cleanup so re-running the suite doesn't pile up demo rows. Skip on master if it fails — DB cleanup can be done manually with `DELETE FROM security_users WHERE username LIKE 'exploit_%';`.
